title: When Arguments Matter
text:
In 1981 Richard Petty, John Cacioppo and Rachel Goldman tested when people are persuaded by good arguments and when they are persuaded by who is speaking. Their participants were students at the University of Missouri, who listened to a recorded message arguing that seniors should have to pass a comprehensive exam in their major in order to graduate.

Three things were varied. For some students, the message said the new exam policy would start the next year at their own university, so it would affect them directly. For others, it would start only in ten years, long after they had left. The arguments were either strong, backed by facts and figures, or weak, based on personal opinion and anecdotes. And the speaker was presented either as an expert, a commission on higher education chaired by a Princeton professor, or as a local high school class.

Students for whom the issue mattered personally were persuaded by strong arguments and unmoved by weak ones, almost regardless of who made them. Students for whom the issue was distant were swayed mostly by the prestige of the source and paid much less attention to the arguments. This became central evidence for the elaboration likelihood model, which holds that people think carefully about a message only when they are motivated and able to.
lesson: When the matter affects them, people judge the argument; when it does not, they judge the speaker. Make your case strong for those who care, and credible for those who do not.
people: Richard Petty, John Cacioppo, Rachel Goldman
source: Petty, R. E., Cacioppo, J. T., and Goldman, R. (1981). Personal involvement as a determinant of argument-based persuasion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 41(5), 847-855.
